claims.text: Rapid quenching of nominal FeCoNiTi produces a dual-phase microstructure containing fcc and hexagonal C14 Laves phases.
The FeCoNiTi alloy has ferromagnetic ordering transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped near 100 Oe because their orbital moments are insufficient.
The C14 Laves phase is Ti-rich, whereas the fcc matrix is Fe/Co/Ni-rich.
Ti moments in the C14 phase couple antiferromagnetically to adjacent Fe, Co, and Ni moments in the fcc phase.
Antiferromagnetic coupling involving Ti suppresses the net ferromagnetic moment and saturation magnetization of the fcc phase.
Replacing Co with antiferromagnetic Cr in AlCoFeNi reduces saturation magnetization by more than 50 percent.
Structural dissimilarity between the fcc and C14 phases contributes to interfacial magnetic effects.
The fcc/C14 interfaces act as strong magnetic domain-wall pinning sites.
Antiferromagnetic exchange at the fcc/C14 interfaces creates local magnetic anisotropy and energy barriers that impede domain-wall motion.
Domain-wall pinning and interfacial anisotropy increase the coercivity beyond the 100 Oe limit of single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni.
Dual-phase FeCoNiTi will exhibit approximately 667 Oe coercivity at 400 K.
Dual-phase FeCoNiTi will have lower saturation magnetization at 400 K than single-phase fcc FeCoNi.
Suppressing C14 formation and producing single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi will return coercivity to approximately 100 Oe.
Annealing can dissolve the C14 phase and produce a single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi control.
DFT with longitudinal spin fluctuations can be used to calculate the spin-resolved density of states at the Fermi level for the fcc phase.
The dual-phase and single-phase variants should be compared using hysteresis, saturation magnetization, spin-density-of-states, and XRD phase-fraction measurements.
The hypothesis is falsified if a C14-free fcc alloy has coercivity above 400 Oe or if calculations show no C14-associated reduction of the fcc magnetic moment.
